body_html:
There are two main ways to say I miss you in Spanish, and which one you use depends mostly on where the other person is from. In Mexico and most of Latin America, people say te extraño. In Spain, the everyday phrase is te echo de menos, literally “I throw you as less”, though te extraño is understood everywhere. Beyond those two, Spanish has a whole set of warmer phrases for partners, family and friends, from me haces falta (I need you here) to cuento los días para verte (I’m counting the days until I see you).

Quick answer
  • Latin America: Te extraño. Spain: Te echo de menos.
  • Stronger: Te extraño muchísimo. Me haces mucha falta.
  • To a group: Los extraño (Latin America) or Os echo de menos (Spain).
  • Reply: Yo también te extraño.
{{toc}}

The main ways to say I miss you in Spanish

SpanishEnglish
Te extraño.I miss you. (Latin America, understood everywhere)
Te echo de menos.I miss you. (Spain)
Te extraño mucho.I miss you a lot.
Te extraño muchísimo.I miss you so much.
Me haces falta.I miss you; I need you here.
Me haces mucha falta.I really miss having you here.
Ya quiero verte.I can’t wait to see you.
Cuento los días para verte.I’m counting the days until I see you.

Me haces falta is especially tender. It comes from hacer falta, “to be needed”, so it says that something is missing from your life without the other person.

Saying it to a partner

With a partner, Spanish allows a lot of warmth. These phrases are common in messages and on the phone:

  • Te extraño, mi amor. I miss you, my love.
  • No dejo de pensar en ti. I can’t stop thinking about you.
  • La casa se siente vacía sin ti. The house feels empty without you.
  • Me muero por verte. I’m dying to see you.
  • Ojalá estuvieras aquí. I wish you were here.

Pair them with a pet name from {{link:spanish-terms-of-endearment|Spanish terms of endearment}}, and if you are apart for a long time, see {{link:long-distance-relationship-spanish|long-distance relationship in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Saying it to family and friends

With family and friends, the same verbs work, with less intensity:

  • Te extraño, mamá. I miss you, Mom.
  • Los extrañamos mucho. We miss you all a lot.
  • ¡Cuánto te he extrañado! I’ve missed you so much! (when you finally see someone)
  • Se te extraña por aquí. We miss you around here. (friendly, light)
  • Extraño nuestras pláticas. I miss our chats. (Mexico)

You can also miss places and things: Extraño la comida de mi abuela (I miss my grandmother’s cooking). Extraño México (I miss Mexico). In Spain: Echo de menos mi pueblo.

How the grammar works

Extrañar is a regular verb that works just like “miss” in English: the person who misses is the subject, and the person missed is the object. Te extraño means “I miss you”; ¿Me extrañas? means “Do you miss me?”

Echar de menos works the same way, but the object pronoun goes before the verb: Te echo de menos, ¿Me echas de menos?

Hacer falta is different. It works like {{link:how-to-use-gustar|gustar}}: the person who is missed is the subject. Me haces falta literally means “you are lacking to me”. So “I miss my kids” becomes Me hacen falta mis hijos, with a plural verb.

{{book:love-slowly}}

A sample message exchange

Ana: Hola, amor. ¿Cómo te fue hoy?
Hi, love. How was your day?

Luis: Bien, pero largo. Te extraño mucho.
Good, but long. I miss you a lot.

Ana: Yo también te extraño. Ya quiero que sea viernes.
I miss you too. I can’t wait for Friday.

Luis: Cuento los días. Me haces mucha falta.
I’m counting the days. I really miss you.

Notice how Ana answers with yo también. You could also say y yo a ti (and I you), which sounds a little more romantic.

For more on texting style and abbreviations like tqm, see {{link:texting-in-spanish|texting in Spanish}}.

Common mistakes

  • Te falto. This means “I’m missing to you”, the opposite. Say Me haces falta or Te extraño.
  • Pierdo a ti. Perder means to lose or to miss a bus, not a person. Say Te extraño.
  • Te echo menos. The de is required: Te echo de menos.
  • Mixing countries. Both phrases are fine, but te echo de menos can sound a bit foreign in Mexico, and te extraño is perfectly natural in Spain too.

The RAE dictionary lists this meaning of extrañar as used across the Spanish-speaking world.

{{image:3}}

Missing someone who has died

The same phrases are used for someone who has passed away, often in the past or with a softer tone: Te extraño todos los días, papá (I miss you every day, Dad). Siempre la vamos a extrañar (We will always miss her). For words to support someone grieving, see {{link:condolences-in-spanish|condolences in Spanish}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Learning to say I miss you in Spanish is really learning three phrases: te extraño, te echo de menos and me haces falta. Choose the one that fits the person and the country, add a little warmth, and your message will land exactly as you mean it. For more moments that matter, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you say I miss you in Spanish?
faq.a: Te extraño in Mexico and most of Latin America, and te echo de menos in Spain.
It means “I miss you” in the sense of “I need you here”. It is warm and tender.

faq.q: How do I say “I miss you too” in Spanish?
faq.a: Yo también te extraño, or more romantically, y yo a ti.

faq.q: Can I say “te extraño” to a friend?
faq.a: Yes. It works for partners, family and friends; the context and tone show the kind of love.

quiz.title: Quick quiz: saying I miss you

questions.q: The most common way to say “I miss you” in Mexico:
questions.explain: Te echo de menos is the usual phrase in Spain.

questions.q: “I miss my kids.” Me ___ falta mis hijos.
questions.explain: The kids are the subject of hacer falta, so the verb is plural.
You are the subject; me is the object.

questions.q: Which phrase is missing a word?

questions.explain: In Latin America, los is used for “you all”.

questions.q: A romantic reply to te extraño:
questions.explain: Y yo a ti or yo también te extraño are natural.
